title: Harden not your hearts (Psalm 94 [95])
hookLine: the psalm that opens the Church's daily prayer: today if you shall hear his voice
tomorrow: Bless the Lord, O my soul (Psalm 102 [103])

lines: A CROSS TRACED ON THE LIPS.
cards: Every morning, in monasteries, convents, rectories and a lot of ordinary kitchens, the Church's daily prayer begins with the same words.

Before any psalm or reading, someone traces a small cross on their lips and says: Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare your praise. It's a line from the Miserere, the psalm from five days ago.
Then, right away, comes a psalm, on most days the same one. It's the doorbell of the whole day's prayer.

teach.b: That opening is called the Invitatory, from the Latin for invitation.
Its usual psalm is Psalm 94 in the Douay, 95 in most Bibles, and it begins exactly like an invitation: "Come let us praise the Lord with joy: let us joyfully sing to God our saviour." Come. Let's go.
It's plural; nobody's praying alone. It moves through God as maker of the deep places of the earth and the mountain peaks, the sea and the dry land.
Then it slows down: "Come let us adore and fall down: and weep before the Lord that made us. For he is the Lord our God: and we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand."

teach.h: TO DAY IF YOU SHALL HEAR HIS VOICE.
teach.b: Then, suddenly, the tone changes: "To day if you shall hear his voice, harden not your hearts."
God himself speaks, and recalls the desert, when their ancestors, thirsty and angry, tested God at a place called Massah and Meribah, testing and quarreling, though they'd seen everything he'd done.

They heard, and their hearts went hard. A warning tucked inside an invitation. The Letter to the Hebrews presses on that one word, today: encourage one another every day, as long as it's still called today.
Every morning, the Church hears it fresh.
Not yesterday. Not some better tomorrow. Today.
And the question it asks is simple: if God spoke to you today, in a person, a moment, a line you read, would you be soft enough to notice?

how: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours begin each day with the Invitatory: 'Lord, open my lips' with a small sign of the cross on the lips, then an antiphon and usually Psalm 94 [95], before the first hour of the day.

o: the call to prayer that opens the Church's day
a written invitation to a parish event
the closing blessing at the end of Mass

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.
p: where the desert people tested God

s: the Church's daily prayer usually opens with the same psalm
the Invitatory, most often Psalm 94 [95]: come let us praise the Lord.
the psalm is only an invitation, with no warning in it
God speaks: harden not your hearts, as in the desert.
Lord, open my lips comes from the Invitatory psalm itself
it comes from the Miserere, Psalm 50 [51].

games.q: you're in the desert, thirsty, and angry at God, even though you've seen the sea split. what did the ancestors in the psalm do?
o: tested God and quarreled, and their hearts went hard.
games.why: at Massah and Meribah they tested God. the psalm turns it into a warning for every morning: today if you shall hear his voice, harden not your hearts.

practice: Before saying anything, to God or to yourself, just listen: the room, the traffic, your own breathing, the small voice in you that says the thing you've been avoiding. Don't answer it yet; just hear it.
Then, if you pray, trace a small cross on your lips and say, Lord, open my lips; if you don't, notice what you heard when you stopped talking.

wordCard.voice: Invitatory. The invitation that opens the Church's daily prayer, with the psalm that says: today, if you hear his voice. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: come, let us rejoice in the Lord, the psalm's first words, the name it's long been known by.

carryVoice: Your line: today, if you hear. The invitation comes new every morning. Day one hundred seventy-six, done.
